title: Carbon permit allocation, carbon neutrality time and climate debt for one country under equal environmental human rights
abstract: This paper introduces the foundations of science and environmental human rights (EHRs) for carbon permit allocation (CPA) of one country, and the hierarchical framework of CPA and corresponding climate debt as well. Then, with the framework of equal EHRs, primary CPA, remaining carbon emission quota (RCEQ), mandatory carbon neutrality time (MCNT), cumulative atmospheric extra warming and climate debt for one country are studied. Observation analysis indicates that each 1000 Gt C of cumulative CO2 emissions is assessed to likely cause a 0.49 °C increase in global mean surface air temperature (GMT) with a range [0.25–0.74]°C, higher than a 0.45 °C with a range [0.27–0.63]°C of the Sixth Assessment Report (AR6) of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) (in: Masson-Delmotte et al. (eds) Climate Change 2021: The physical science basis. Contribution of Working Group I to the sixth assessment report of the intergovernmental panel on climate change. Cambridge University Press, 2021). Observation and a climate-carbon model (CCM) demonstrate that the long-term warming in GMT since 1850 are the result of cumulative human emissions. Therefore, we further introduce a new carbon accounting system, the EPC (an equal per capita carbon quota under equal EHRs). For the 2 °C threshold and 2050 global carbon neutrality initiative, as of 2022, the USA, Canada, Russia, the UK, Germany, and Australia (C6 for short) no longer have any allowable carbon emission space, their total carbon emission deficits is up to 656.15 Gt C, their MCNTs are 1936, 1928, 1959, 1966, 1966, and 1988, respectively, and the cumulative climate debts of the USA and C6 have reached as high as about US $ 34.9 and 59.1 trillion (calculated at US $90 per tCO2), respectively. The cumulative atmospheric extra warmings caused by the USA and C6 countries are ~ 0.194 and 0.328 °C, respectively, accounting for ~ 49% and 82% of the total extra warming caused, respectively, and explain 15.3% and 25.8% of the GMT increase since 1850, respectively, resulting in a serious deterioration of the EHRs in these countries with significant negative national EHRs indices. The China’s RCEQ is 423.23 Gt C, and its MCNT will be in 2061, indicating that the China’s commitment to achieving carbon neutrality before 2060 is fully in line with this outcome.
problem: Existing methods for assigning climate change responsibility are often unscientific and unfair, as they ignore factors like equal environmental human rights, historical emissions, land-use change, and demographic differences, leading to inequitable carbon permit allocations and climate debt calculations.
method: This paper introduces a carbon accounting system based on an equal per capita carbon quota under equal environmental human rights (EHRs) to calculate national carbon permits, mandatory carbon neutrality times, and climate debt.
task: The task is to establish a framework based on equal environmental human rights to calculate countries' carbon permit allocation, mandatory carbon neutrality time, and corresponding climate debt, thereby assessing their historical climate responsibilities.

kg_extraction_triplets.target_entity_instance: a simple atmospheric CO2 concentration model
kg_extraction_triplets.paragraph: To theoretically depict the climate response (global atmospheric CO2 concentration and GMT) to anthropogenic cumulative carbon emissions, we developed a simple CCM, which consists of a simple atmospheric CO2 concentration model and a simple GMT model.

To theoretically depict the climate response (global atmospheric CO2 concentration and GMT) to anthropogenic cumulative carbon emissions, we developed a simple CCM, which consists of a simple atmospheric CO2 concentration model and a simple GMT model.

Figures 4a, b show observed and simulated atmospheric CO2 concentration and GMT for 1850–2023, respectively. As shown in Fig. 4a, the model effectively simulates the historical changes in the annually atmospheric CO2 concentration observed, reflecting that these changes are the result of cumulative human emissions.

The simulated GMT of the CCM well demonstrates the historical growth changes of the observed GMT (Fig. 4b), also reflecting that the long-term warming changes in the GMT are the result of cumulative human emissions.
Here we employ the modified Euler method of order 2 (Burden and Faires 2011) to numerically solve the CCM.
